title: Unit 8: Basic Mineral Development
sub: Reading: pages 115–124  ·  20 points  ·  15 minutes  ·  Closed book
instructions: Answer every question. For multiple choice, circle the single best answer. Write short answers in complete sentences.

questions.stem: What determines which element an atom is?
choices: The number of protons in the nucleus
The number of electrons in orbit
The total mass of the atom
The number of neutrons in the nucleus
questions.why: p. 116 — all atoms of a particular element are identical, and the proton count is what fixes the identity.

questions.stem: An atom that loses an electron becomes
choices: an anion with a negative charge
a cation with a positive charge
questions.why: p. 117 — losing a negatively charged electron leaves more protons than electrons, so the net charge is positive. Gaining an electron produces an anion.

questions.stem: Which group of minerals makes up most of Earth’s crust?
questions.why: p. 116 — carbonates and native elements are also named as important, but chiefly for their usefulness to society rather than their abundance.

questions.stem: Streak is considered a more reliable identification property than color because
choices: streak is easier to observe than color
questions.why: p. 119 — two minerals of the same color may leave different colored streaks. Pyrite looks gold but streaks blackish, while real gold streaks golden yellow.

questions.stem: On the Mohs scale of mineral hardness, which mineral is the softest?
questions.why: p. 121 — talc can be scratched by all other materials. The full scale runs talc, gypsum, calcite, fluorite, apatite, feldspar, quartz, topaz, corundum, diamond.

questions.stem: Mica breaks along very closely spaced flat planes that yield thin sheets. This property is called
questions.why: pp. 121–122 — cleavage follows lines of weakness in the mineral’s structure. Calcite cleaves in three directions into rhombs, and galena into true cubes.

questions.stem: Color is usually the most reliable physical property for identifying a mineral.
questions.why: Color is the most eye-catching property but usually the least reliable. Pure quartz is colorless, while amethyst is the same mineral colored purple by traces of iron. (pp. 117–118)

questions.stem: Fracture is not always the same within a single mineral, because fracture is not determined by the mineral’s structure.
questions.why: p. 123 — unlike cleavage, which follows structural planes of weakness. Quartz is known for fracturing into smooth curved surfaces.

questions.stem: The International Mineralogical Association sets requirements a substance must meet to be considered a distinct mineral. Name three of them.
questions.answer: It must occur naturally, be solid, have an ordered internal (crystallographic) structure, and have a fairly well-defined chemical composition.
questions.rubric: 1 pt for each of any three. (1) Naturally occurring, formed by natural geological processes — this excludes anything made by human activity or by living beings, such as seashells or tungsten carbide. (2) A solid in its natural occurrence. (3) A well-defined crystallographic structure, or more generally an ordered atomic arrangement. (4) A fairly well-defined chemical composition. (p. 124)

questions.stem: Explain the difference between cleavage and fracture, and give one example of a mineral that shows each.
questions.answer: Cleavage is the tendency of a mineral to break along structural planes of weakness, producing smooth surfaces. Fracture is any break that does not follow a cleavage plane.
questions.rubric: 1 pt cleavage defined — breakage along certain planes determined by the mineral’s internal structure, yielding smooth surfaces. 1 pt fracture defined — a break not along a cleavage plane, and therefore not fixed by structure. 1 pt for one valid example of each. Cleavage: mica (one plane, thin sheets), calcite (three planes, rhombs), galena or halite (three planes at right angles, cubes). Fracture: quartz (smooth curved surfaces), chrysotile (splintery), metals (jagged edges). (pp. 121–123)
